podcast.body: This major hit was originally written by Holland, Dozier, and Holland for The Marvelettes, but Gladys Horton rejected it as "too simplistic." It was then given to The Supremes, who were internally referred to as "the no-hit Supremes" at the time. "Holland, Doge and Holland had written a song for them, but Gladys didn't like it."

podcast.body: This song was the winner of the 1964 Billboard Song of the Summer. It was a breakthrough hit for The Supremes and the first of their 12 number ones, establishing them as the most successful girl group in chart history. "Not only did this song take the title, it was the breakthrough hit for the most successful girl group in chart history. The first of 12 number ones for the Supremes."

podcast.body: This iconic song was initially conceived by Holland-Dozier-Holland for a proposed Marvelettes album, featuring a simple, repetitive 8-bar verse without a bridge, chorus, or middle eight. Rejected by The Marvelettes, the backing track was passed to The Supremes, who were pressured to record it. The session was fraught with conflict over who would sing lead (Mary Wilson initially, then Diana Ross by executive decision), Diana's dissatisfaction with the song's key and "terrible" quality, and the eventual spontaneous "baby baby" backing vocals. Despite the group's unhappiness, Barry Gordy immediately recognized its hit potential and promised them future success. "Gordy, much to Ross's shock, was convinced it was a hit, and said to them, cheer up everybody, from now on you're the big hit Supremes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
